title: Dark Matter: Maybe the problem was never finding the right universe (Recap)
excerpt: Jason searches for a life beyond the Box, Daniela reconnects with her father, and Charlie makes a dangerous choice
content:
After devoting an entire episode to one of the many Jasons left behind — and delivering, for me, one of Dark Matter’s most beautiful chapters — the series returns to the Dessen family in “What the Universe Is Made Of.” But something has changed. The Box remains at the center of everything, naturally, but this week’s question is no longer simply where it can take them. It is something else: after everything that has happened, can Jason, Daniela and Charlie still figure out who they are without it?

Daniela begins by searching for an answer in the past. She goes looking for Gabriel Vargas, the man she considers her father, although we learn that he is actually her stepfather. Gabriel entered her life when she was eight, after the death of her biological father, and became the person who filled that emotional role from then on.

It is a revealing choice. Daniela has spent the season trying to understand whether she can remain married to Jason after everything she has lived through, but when she needs distance, she does not seek another universe, an adventure or even a solution. She seeks her father.

Gabriel lives in isolation, and Daniela stays with him for a while, drawing, painting and trying to recover a version of herself that existed before the Box. He realizes that something is wrong and offers one of those apparently simple lines that, in Dark Matter, usually carries another meaning: what we refuse to face does not simply disappear because we decide to bury it.

Except there is one small problem. Gabriel knows his daughter. He even recognizes her brushstrokes in the painting. So he knows that the woman standing in front of him is Daniela. But he has just spoken to Daniela on the phone. His daughter.The one who lives in San Francisco.

Gabriel initially believes he may be suffering some kind of neurological problem until Daniela finally tells him the truth. Yes, his daughter is still in San Francisco. And yes, the woman standing before him is also Daniela. For the first time, she tells someone outside the Dessen family about the multiverse. It matters because Daniela has spent most of this story being forced to accept an impossible reality created by the Jasons. Now, finally, she turns her experience into narrative. She gets to tell her own story.

Jason, meanwhile, meets another Amanda. Not Amanda Lucas, the one we know, but Amanda Azevedo, the owner of the restaurant where Charlie is working. The face is the same; the life is completely different. This Amanda wanted to study medicine, but abandoned that dream after her mother, during a manic episode, bought the restaurant using their house as collateral and spent the money that had been meant for her daughter’s education.

It is a small story that perfectly summarizes the logic of Dark Matter: change a few circumstances and the same person can end up living an entirely different life. And Amanda is exactly the person who tells Jason something he needs to hear. Charlie is growing up. His marriage is in crisis. He cannot build his entire identity around being a husband and a father. Because that may have been one of Jason’s greatest traps from the beginning. For years, he looked at Jason2 as the man he might have become: the brilliant scientist, recognized and accomplished, capable of turning an impossible theory into the Box. Jason chose Daniela and Charlie. The problem is that he also turned that choice into a kind of absolute identity. Now he is beginning to understand that one thing does not necessarily have to exclude the other.

When he reconnects with Blair, the conversation finally brings Jason back to science — and this may be where the episode plants its most interesting idea. This is not just any Blair. It is the Blair who entered the Box during Jason2’s experiments and became trapped in that universe overrun by insect-like creatures. She eventually managed to escape and deliberately chose a less technologically advanced world, one where she could disappear, start over, and live without digital traces everywhere.

And yet, in a practically infinite multiverse, she finds Daniela. Then she finds Jason. What are the odds? That is where this week’s hypothesis begins: what if the people who travel through the Box become entangled in some way?

Jason has been studying quantum entanglement precisely because he wants to discover how to permanently block access to that universe. Destroying the physical structure does not solve the problem. They already know that. If someone in another reality creates a connection to that world, another Box can simply appear. So perhaps the Box cannot be destroyed. Perhaps the connection has to be broken. And Blair raises an even more unsettling possibility: if particles can remain linked regardless of distance, could something similar happen to the people moving between universes? Maybe Jason, Amanda, Blair, Leighton, Daniela, and the others keep finding one another because their lives became connected in a way not even the multiverse can undo. Or, as Jason suggests, perhaps they were always connected. The Box merely made it visible.

It is a beautiful and dangerous idea for the series because it completely changes the meaning of coincidence in Dark Matter. The multiverse may be infinite, but perhaps relationships are not. Blair takes Jason to an academic event and, surrounded once again by scientists, professors, and researchers, he finally admits something he almost seems embarrassed to say: he wants to be a scientist again. He wants to do research. He wants to publish. He wants to discover something. And when Jason worries that he is simply trying to occupy the other Jason’s place, Blair reminds him of something very simple: that intelligence belongs to him too.

Perhaps one of the season’s central questions is exactly this. Jason spent so long defining Jason2 as “the scientist” and himself as “the man who chose his family” that he forgot they both came from the same person. Choosing Daniela did not erase the scientist. And choosing science does not have to mean abandoning Daniela. The episode also saves one of its most delicate scenes for Jason and Charlie. Jason finally tells his son that, during one of his travels, he found a universe where Max survived. Max received a heart transplant. Charlie immediately wants to know what his brother was like. Jason tries to describe him: smart, funny, empathetic, sometimes difficult. But eventually he finds the only word that really matters. Perfect.

There is something very beautiful in the way the series handles this information. Jason does not suggest finding Max. He does not propose opening the Box again. He does not turn the boy’s existence into another mission. He simply tells Charlie that his brother existed somewhere, and that he had a life. Maybe Jason is finally beginning to understand that knowing another world exists does not mean we have to possess it. But while Jason begins to imagine a life beyond the Box, Leighton is doing exactly the opposite.

At the event, Blair encounters Leighton Vance and initially does not know whether she is looking at another version of him. She is not. It is the Leighton she knew. He remembers her. He tells her that he kept her cat, Murphy, after Blair disappeared and admits that he has been living in that universe for nearly two years. And he has done something remarkable.

Leighton realized that this reality was technologically behind and began introducing knowledge from more advanced worlds. Microprocessors. Computers. Technology that should not yet exist there. Naturally, he became extremely rich. But money was only the beginning. Leighton takes Blair into Chicago’s old underground freight tunnels and explains the logic of his project. Very old infrastructure has a better chance of existing in roughly the same place across different realities.

And then he shows her what he is building. A new structure connected to the Box — bigger, more complex, and seemingly designed not for one person searching for another world, but to turn interdimensional travel into something organized. Industrial. Maybe even permanent. Blair looks at it and can only ask the question we are all thinking: what the hell is that? The answer will have to wait until next week.

But before that, Dark Matter leaves one more small bomb inside the Dessen family itself. Charlie takes a flashlight. He takes the drug required to enter the Box. And he goes in alone. The irony is impossible to miss. Jason and Daniela have spent two seasons trying to protect their son from the consequences of the Box. Perhaps they never realized that growing up surrounded by infinite universes might give Charlie exactly what Jason has: the need to open the door. The question now is not only where Charlie goes. It is what he is looking for.

After six episodes, Dark Matter finally seems to be moving beyond the fantasy that a perfect universe is waiting behind one particular door. Jason wants to return to science. Daniela needs to discover who she is after everything she has endured. Charlie begins his own journey. Blair realizes that the travelers may be linked. And Leighton has done what humanity always seems to do when it discovers something extraordinary: turn discovery into a system.

The Box began as a machine capable of answering one intimate question: what if I had chosen a different life? Leighton may be about to answer another, much more frightening one. What if we could choose the entire world?
